Psychology in film, literature and music

1984 and Newspeak: does language shape thought?

Orwell imagined a language designed to make certain ideas unthinkable. Science has qualified that idea.

In Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), George Orwell describes Newspeak, a language the Party keeps shrinking so that, without words to express them, ideas such as rebellion become impossible to think.

Sapir, Whorf and the debate

The idea recalls the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, according to which language determines how we think. In its strong form it has been rejected: we can think things we have no words for and learn new concepts. But a weaker version has support: language influences some aspects of perception and memory.

For example, Russian speakers, who have separate words for light and dark blue, tell them apart slightly faster. And speakers of Kuuk Thaayorre in Australia, who always orient themselves using compass directions instead of "left" and "right", have an extraordinary sense of direction.

References

  1. Winawer, J. et al. (2007). Russian blues reveal effects of language on color discrimination. PNAS, 104(19), 7780–7785.
  2. Boroditsky, L. y Gaby, A. (2010). Remembrances of times East. Psychological Science, 21(11), 1635–1639.
